newsitem.title: CAMBODIA: Problems arise as world awaits fate of Pol Pot.
newsitem.headline: Problems arise as world awaits fate of Pol Pot.

text.p: Cambodia's First Prime Minister said on Sunday he wanted to see Khmer Rouge leader Pol Pot moved out of the jungle where he was being held by members of a rebel splinter faction which captured him this week.
Prince Norodom Ranariddh told reporters Pol Pot should be moved from the jungle base of Anlong Veng, where he was being held by the Khmer Rouge renegades, for security reasons.
"We should move him out as soon as possible ... for security reasons," Ranariddh said.
The prince said Pol Pot was now in Anlong Veng and he was very sick. The 69-year-old Pol Pot has long suffered from malaria.

The prince did not elaborate on why he felt Pol Pot should be moved for reasons of security but government officials said negotiators were headed to the northern guerrilla zone on Sunday to iron out problems over Pol Pot's fate.
One senior officer said there was still factional disagreement in the fractured Khmer Rouge as to what should happen to Pol Pot.
"The situation in Anlong Veng is very complicated," said the army general who declined to be identified.
"As far as I know Pol Pot's supporters are trying to liberate him from the the breakaway group," the general, speaking by telephone from northern Cambodia, told Reuters.
Another military official confirmed that there were difficulties to overcome before Pol Pot could be brought to justice.
"We must clear some problems," said the military official. He declined to elaborate.

Deputy chief of general staff Nhiek Bun Chhay, who has spearheaded talks with a Khmer Rouge faction which broke with Pol Pot earlier this month, was travelling north in an attempt to seal the veteran guerrilla supremo's fate, officals said.

Ranariddh said the hated Khmer Rouge chief woud eventually be brought to Phnom Penh and moves were under way to bring him before an international tribunal for the crimes he committed during his 1975-79 "killing fields" rule.
An aide to the prince said on Sunday he was not expecting to see Pol Pot in the Cambodian capital soon, but he said he was confident the hardline communist would eventually be brought to jutice.
"I think not so soon, but for sure, we'll see him," the aide said. "The Cambodian people need to see the proof."
Pol Pot fled Anglong Veng earlier this month after ordering the slaughter of his defence chief and almost a dozen members of his family.

Pol Pot, whose Khmer Rouge government was responsible for the death of more than a million Cambodians, has not been seen in public since 1980, two years after his overthrow at the hands of an invading Vietnamese army.
He was sentenced to death in absentia by a Phnom Penh court soon after his overthrow.

Pol Pot led a Cambodian peasant army to victory against the U.S.-backed Lon Nol republic in 1975, or Year Zero, as the Khmer Rouge called it. They immediately embarked on a bloody restructuring of society.
Pol Pot's guerrillas emptied Phnom Penh at gunpoint, forcing the sick from their beds. Women, children and the elderly were ordered into the countryside and put to work in labour camps.
More than one million people were executed as enemies of Pol Pot's utopian revolution or died of disease, starvation or overwork during their reign.
